news_drafts.headline: Cambridgeshire Pension Fund: KPMG sets £49m materiality for its 2025-26 audit
news_drafts.lead:
Cambridgeshire Pension Fund's external auditor, the accountancy firm KPMG, has set materiality for its audit of the fund's 2025-26 accounts at £49m. Materiality is the size of error that an auditor treats as large enough to matter to a reader of the accounts. The Pension Fund Board noted the audit plan at its meeting on 3 July 2026, and the minutes record: "Materiality had been set at £49 million."

KPMG calculated the figure as 1% of the fund's total draft assets as at 31 March 2025. Its plan lists two significant risks: management override of controls, and the valuation of level three assets, which are investments with no quoted market price.

According to the minutes, officers do not expect material differences on the fund's private equity investments.

news_drafts.headline: Cambridgeshire schools funding: historic commitments fall from £1.21m to £968k for 2027/28
news_drafts.lead:
Papers for Cambridgeshire's Schools Forum show the council's historic commitments falling from £1.21m in 2026/27 to an estimate of £968k in 2027/28. They sit within the dedicated schools grant (DSG), the government grant that funds schools. The schools funding update for the forum's meeting on 6 November describes the change as a further 20% reduction.

The paper says the planned underspend on historic commitments is to "contribute towards DSG deficit recovery". A DSG deficit is an overspend on that grant, usually on support for children with special educational needs.

The commitments are part of the grant's central school services block, which the table puts at £5.341m in 2026/27 and £5.099m in 2027/28. The paper also says that funding for historic commitments that have now ended will be taken as a direct saving.
news_drafts.paper_title: Item 7 Appendix 1 - Schools Funding Update - November 2026

news_drafts.headline: Cambridgeshire forecasts £159.8m schools grant deficit for 2026-27; government yet to accept plan
news_drafts.lead:
Cambridgeshire County Council forecasts that its dedicated schools grant (DSG), the government grant that funds schools, will show a cumulative deficit of £159.8m at the end of 2026-27. The deficit is an overspend on that grant. It opened the year at £96.5m and is forecast to rise by £63.3m during 2026-27, according to the period 5 finance monitoring report before the Strategy, Resources and Performance Committee on 22 October.

The report estimates the deficit will cost the council £6.3m in debt financing in 2026-27. It says the deficit reduces the cash the council can use for internal borrowing, which means paying for spending from its own cash instead of taking a loan. In February, government said it would fund up to 90% of historical deficits to the end of 2025-26 if councils submitted a recovery plan. The council submitted its plan in June. The report says Department for Education advisers gave positive feedback on the draft, but government did not accept the submission and asked for more information. The council plans to resubmit in October. No date has been confirmed for any grant.

The council's budget-planning paper says it expects to fund 10% of the deficit to the end of 2025-26, with part already provided for in reserves, and sets aside £6.0m for this in 2027-28. Its risk register says the statutory override, a temporary government rule that keeps a schools-funding deficit off the main balance sheet, has been confirmed to 31 March 2028. It says funding for 2026-27 and 2027-28 remains uncertain, and that the council holds £7.5m in reserves.

findings.headline: Three admission bodies joined the Fund and five admission agreements ceased since the last Pension Committee meeting.
findings.detail: The new admissions include Accent Catering Services Limited (Four Cs MAT), Alliance Cleaning Limited (Fawcett Primary School) and Peterborough Culture, Heritage, Learning and Leisure Limited. The cessations include Cambridgeshire & Peterborough Clinical Commissioning Group, along with several schools and trust-related bodies. Two earlier cessations received updates.
findings.matters: Cessations trigger exit debits or credits, so a finance director can use the cessation count and the named bodies to track the Fund's exposure to employer exits.
findings.figures: 3 admitted bodies; 5 ceasing admission bodies; 2 updated earlier cessations
findings.quote: Three admitted bodies have joined the Fund since the last meeting of the Pension Committee.

findings.headline: Proposed RAG criteria for risk 4b tie the rating to the funding level, with Green at 120% or above, Amber from 100% to below 120%, and Red below 100%.
findings.detail: The change incorporates the latest quarterly funding update, including the funding level at the end of the most recent quarter and movements since the 2025 actuarial valuation. The paper says the aim is a clear and consistent method for monitoring funding risk. The paper does not state the current funding level.
findings.matters: A published funding-level threshold for the Green, Amber and Red ratings gives a reference point for comparing how funds grade the same risk.
findings.figures: Green at or above 120%; Amber above 100% and below 120%; Red below 100%

findings.headline: Employer contributions were 99.9% received on time for the reporting period, matching the annual compliance rate of 99.9%.
findings.detail: The paper reports 99.8% received on time in May and June 2026 and 100% in July and August 2026. Late payment details are in an exempt appendix. No material breaches were reported in the period.
findings.matters: Employer contribution timeliness is a key indicator of covenant and cash-flow health for the Fund.
findings.figures: 99.9% on time (reporting period); 99.9% annual compliance; 99.8% (May and June 2026); 100% (July and August 2026)
findings.quote: maintaining a consistent annual compliance rate of 99.9%.

findings.headline: Divorce quotation (CETV) calculations were suspended from 19 May 2026 to 15 June 2026 while updated GAD factors were awaited.
findings.detail: The suspension followed changes to the SCAPE discount rate. Divorce casework could not progress during the suspension, which created a backlog and reduced KPI performance in June. Processing resumed once the revised factors were received.
findings.matters: Changes to GAD factors can halt a whole class of cases, and the paper shows how long one such pause lasted.
findings.quote: temporary suspension of divorce quotation (CETV) calculations between 19 May 2026 and 15 June

findings.headline: Continued compliance against the Pensions Regulator's General Code of Practice has been reprofiled to 31 May 2027.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the lack of progress to competing statutory priorities. The rolling plan that the activity covers is now due for completion by 31 May 2027.
findings.matters: A Regulator Code of Practice compliance deadline that has slipped is a governance point other funds may face under similar pressure.
findings.quote: No further progress has been made in this area due to competing statutory priorities.

daily_post.headline: Employee retention remains above target at 90%, indicating staff stability despite organisational change
daily_post.lead: Retaining staff maintains service continuity and avoids costly recruitment and training; stable retention above target despite announced organisational change is a positive signal that people management and change communication are working effectively.
